**The Weight of Empty Spaces**

There’s a quiet ache in the way the world moves when no one is watching. It’s the hum of a refrigerator in an empty kitchen, the flicker of a streetlamp against a curtain at 3 AM, the way a name lingers on your tongue long after the person has left. These are the ghosts of presence—the echoes of things that were, or could have been.

I’ve always been fascinated by the spaces between. Not the grand silences of cathedrals or the hush of a library, but the small, personal absences. The half-drunk cup of coffee left on the counter, still warm. The unanswered text that sits in your inbox like a judgment. The way a room feels different when someone you love walks out of it, even if they’ll be back in five minutes.

We fill these gaps with noise—music, podcasts, the endless scroll of social media—because silence is a vacuum, and vacuums have a way of pulling things in. They make us confront what we’ve been avoiding. The loneliness. The regret. The quiet realization that maybe, just maybe, we’re not as connected as we pretend to be.

I wonder if other people feel this too. If they wake up in the middle of the night and stare at the ceiling, wondering how their life got so heavy without them noticing. If they’ve ever stood in a room full of people and felt utterly alone. If they’ve ever loved someone so much it hurt to breathe when they weren’t around.

Love is just another kind of absence, isn’t it? The fear of losing someone is the weight of their potential absence pressing down on you. And when they’re gone, even for a little while, it’s like a limb has been amputated—you don’t realize how much you relied on their presence until the phantom limb starts to ache.

I’ve been thinking a lot about time lately. Not in the abstract, philosophical way, but in the way it *feels*. How a single day can stretch into eternity when you’re waiting for something—good or bad. How a year can vanish in a blink when you’re not paying attention. How some moments feel like they last forever, even though they’re over in an instant.

Time is a thief, but it’s also a liar. It tells us that things will get better, that we’ll move on, that the pain will fade. And sometimes it does. But other times, it doesn’t. Sometimes the absence leaves a scar, and the scar itches when the weather changes.

I used to think that the goal was to fill every empty space with something meaningful. A hobby. A relationship. A purpose. But now I’m not so sure. Maybe some spaces are meant to stay empty. Maybe they’re not voids to be filled, but invitations—to sit with the discomfort, to feel the weight of what isn’t there, to remember that absence is just as much a part of life as presence.

The other day, I found an old notebook from high school. Flipping through it, I was struck by how young I was, how sure I was of things that turned out to be wrong. I laughed at my teenage angst, at the dramatic way I wrote about heartbreak and dreams. But then I realized something: I still feel those things. Not in the same way, not with the same intensity, but the core of it—the fear of not being enough, the longing for something more—is still there.

That’s the thing about absence. It’s not just about what’s missing. It’s about what remains. The echoes. The imprints. The way a person can shape you even after they’re gone.

I don’t know what to do with that knowledge. Maybe nothing. Maybe just acknowledging it is enough. Maybe the point isn’t to fill the spaces, but to learn how to carry them.

Because in the end, we’re all just walking around with these hollows inside us, trying to figure out how to live with the weight of what isn’t there. And maybe that’s okay. Maybe the spaces are where the magic happens—the quiet moments of reflection, the unexpected bursts of creativity, the sudden clarity when you realize you’ve been holding your breath without knowing it.

So here’s to the empty spaces. May they never be filled with anything less than what they deserve.
